solution: To address these challenges, in this paper, we propose Edgent, a framework that leverages edge computing for DNN collaborative inference through device-edge synergy. We implement Edgent prototype based on the Raspberry Pi and the desktop PC and the extensive experimental evaluations demonstrate Edgent’s effectiveness in enabling ondemand low-latency edge intelligence. On this issue, in this paper, we exploit the edge computing paradigm and propose Edgent, a low-latency co-inference framework via device-edge synergy.
experiments: Through the exhaustive search on points, we can figure out the optimal partition point with the minimum latency of the i-th exit point. Since the model partitioning does not affect the inference accuracy, we can successively test the DNN inference with different exit layers (i.e., with different precision) and find the model with the maximum accuracy while satisfying the latency requirement at the same time. As the regression models for layer-wise latency prediction have been trained in advance, Algorithm 1 mainly involves linear search operations and can be completed very quickly (no more than 1ms in our experiment).
limitations: Essentially, the earlyexit mechanism involves a latency-accuracy tradeoff. To strike a balance on the tradeoff with the existing resources, Edgent makes a joint optimization on both DNN partitioning and DNN right-sizing in an on-demand manner.
futureDirections: For the future work, our proposed framework can be further combined with existing model compression techniques to accelerate DNN inference.

In this paper, we propose DiffTry as a mechanism for service differentiation and load control using retries.
experiments: DiffTry: Differential Retries DiffTry (Differential Retries) is a simple and stateless mechanism for differential operation of retries across transaction classes, yielding differentiation (and prioritization) in their rejection rates.
Requests are labeled by priority, either High (e.g., premium or latencysensitive users) or Low (e.g., a bypassing user or batch job), and Service A retries them after timeouts or errors.

This selective persistence significantly improves their goodput: even when both classes contribute 50% of the input load, high-priority transactions account for about 85% of successful completions, corresponding to a throughput improvement of about 70%.
